title: Standing
dimensions: height: 168 cm (66 1/8 in.); Diameter: 8 cm (3 1/8 in.)
provenance:
1993–2022 | Collection of the Artist
2022–2023 | (Artstellar Gallery, Seoul, South Korea, sold to Celeste Myers)
2023–2024 | Celeste Myers, Hudson, OH, given to  the Cleveland Museum of Art
2024– | The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OH
description: The artist ground a block of steel to sculpt human figures. Instead of the most common casting technique, Kim chose grinding to demonstrate intense physical labor that deeply involved civilization. Standing was one of the three sculptures Kim presented to an outdoor exhibition in London in 1997, but all three of them were stolen once. While the other two were long lost, this work was fortuitously recovered. Kim recounts that traumatic incident as his moment to rethink steel powder, the leftover of grinding, as the primary media for his later works. In this sense, Standing bears a poignant moment of the artist’s departure for new artistic possibilities.

title: The Intermediate—Naturalized Klangkoerper
materials: Artificial straw, steel stand, powder coating, artificial plants, artificial fruits, artificial vegetables, plastic twine, Indian bells, fringes, casters
credit: Purchased with funds donated by Scott Mueller
provenance:
2016–? | Collection of the artist
?–2018 | (Greene Naftali Gallery, New York, NY, sold to the Cleveland Museum of Art)
June 5, 2018– | The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OH
description: The Intermediate – Naturalized Klangkoerper uses contemporary mass-produced materials—in the “readymade” tradition of modernist art—to conjure folklore and history from the artist’s native South Korea. Its anthropomorphic straw form is suggestive of Korean straw dolls popular in folklore rituals, and the bells integrated throughout the work evoke Korean shaman rituals in which the shaman, almost exclusively women in the Joseon dynasty (1392-1910), would ring bronze bells to communicate with the spiritual world.

title: Umber-Black
provenance:
?–2022 | (PKM Gallery, Seoul, South Korea, sold to the Cleveland Museum of Art)
2022– | The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OH
description: The dark pillars that extend the height of the canvas in Yun Hyong Keun's Umber-Black exemplify the type of work for which the artist was most celebrated. The composition seems simple, yet the process was long and complex. After adding layers of paint—often applying the next coat before the last one had dried—Yun diluted the pigments, allowing them to seep into the fibers of the coarse linen. According to the artist, blank spaces between the pillars evoke a pathway toward “the gate of heaven and earth.” Yet Yun’s paintings do not depict a peaceful cosmos. They were a sanctuary where Yun could escape anger toward the prevailing injustice of South Korea’s military dictatorship in the 1970s and 1980s.

title: Bad Heads Fuck (2)
description: Held most often in stadiums, mass games in South Korea are highly regimented spectacles in which tens of thousands of performers participate. Based on the artist’s memories from his days as a student, these games took countless hours of compulsory practice and disciplined participants to express one idea in apparent unison. Here, matches represent a crowd of villains who have been invited to play a mass game. Like much of Kim’s work, these drawings include words and narratives that intensely engage the viewer’s imagination. In sequence, they follow a scenario with a beginning, a climax, and a resolution. The artist leaves it to the viewer to reconcile the rigidity of the sticks with the fluidity of the writing and the making of the mandala. This gap between matter and image ends the game by paralleling the complex nature of the villain: an individual who has drifted away from humanity’s ideals.

title: Study for "A Rock That Was Taught it Was a Bird"
originalTitle: Study for "A Rock That Was Taught it Was a Bird"
description: This drawing relates to relates to Kim Beom's mixed-media installation, A Rock that was Taught it Was a Bird (2010), also part of the Cleveland Museum of Art's collection. In the study, Kim envisioned the configuration of his project, which features a ready-made sculpture made from a stone and tree bough, a table, and a video monitor. The artist often works between two- and three-dimensional media as a way to question and comment on authoritarianism.

title: The K-12 Art School for Chicago
originalTitle: The K-12 Art School for Chicago
description: This project imagines a K–12 school for arts and visual culture located on the remaining parcel of unoccupied space between the Art Institute of Chicago’s historical building and Modern Wing, spanning the railway tracks. Drawing on the resources of the museum and Millennium Park, the building also promotes an active learning experience, merging classroom, studio, and circulation space in a continuous ribbon within the organic structure. Yoo suggested the growth of the students in this cooperative environment as a vigorous vine incorporating a great variety of different disciplines. Sung Suk Yoo is an architectural designer at Gensler Los Angeles and is currently working on the mixed-use Yongsan International Business District Project in Seoul, South Korea.
